A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AMICL and residual attention stream research. Text, equations, figures, tables, and all appendices are readable. Retained material can be matched across section and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original AMICL simulations, two-layer Transformer training experiments, and 8M-parameter language-model results on TinyStories and indirect object identification, including appendix sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds 1B-parameter language-model evaluations, IOI-Hard results, and architectural control experiments in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The AMICL assignments and layer-to-layer query, key, and value residual operations remain unchanged. The 1B model applies the existing residual-values method in another model configuration; the value-projection removals are control experiments rather than revisions to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Section 5 adds pretraining on English Nemotron-CC-HQ documents and evaluation on ARC, PIQA, OpenBookQA, and HellaSwag. IOI-Hard adds a distinct contextual retrieval scenario involving 25 sentences and multiple name, place, and object associations. The original synthetic tasks and TinyStories/IOI coverage remain.

E2.justification: The matched synthetic comparisons retain the classic Transformer and query/key residual variants. Language-model comparisons still use the classic architecture against residual values, including at 1B scale. Appendix B introduces separate architectural controls without expanding these head-to-head comparator sets.

E3.justification: New experiments use 1B-parameter models trained for 40,000 iterations on approximately 84 billion tokens, with batch size 512 and context length 4,096. Evaluation adds single- and five-shot benchmark accuracy and 1,000 generated IOI-Hard prompts. Appendix B also introduces one-layer control configurations; the original experiments' stated settings remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests four one-layer architectures without learned value projections, varying ReLU depth and placement. These controls examine whether that simpler AMICL-inspired construction supports ICL and how architecture affects learning trajectories. The existing AMICL parameter sweeps and accuracy-threshold analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 adds a paired t-test using benchmark accuracies across training checkpoints, alongside correlation reporting. The original four-seed synthetic experiments and three-instance language-model reporting remain unchanged. Independent repeated-training uncertainty is not reported for the new 1B comparison.

E6.justification: New 1B results show gains concentrated on ARC and OpenBookQA, little change on PIQA and HellaSwag, and a clearer IOI-Hard advantage (Figures 5, 6, and 14). Original numerical tables are unchanged, but Figure 3's IC2 loss changes from rising above 12 to falling near zero. The unchanged IOI table also receives inaccurate new percentage summaries of approximately 590% improvement and 60% reduction.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 changes the stated domain of AMICL's parameter a from positive reals to arbitrary reals, while retaining the tested range and chosen value. The equations remain mathematically equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added. Most additional reasoning is conceptual motivation.

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly extends the demonstrated model scale from 8M to both 8M and 1B parameters and describes larger-model gains as improved performance more generally. AMICL, faster emergence of ICL, and residual value streams remain the central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving auto- versus hetero-association, preservation of representations across layers, and strong IOI differences despite similar training losses. It proposes specific hippocampal ablation hypotheses and explicitly qualifies broader applicability through task-specific gains and unresolved scalability and cost trade-offs (Sections 6.1–6.3).

D1.justification: Section 5 adds substantial architecture, tokenizer, precision, optimizer, training-schedule, and IOI-Hard generation details. The code-access disclosure is retained. Some new schedule information conflicts internally: the prose specifies 500 warmup and 5,000 cooldown steps, while Table 4 gives 1% and 10% of a 40,000-step run.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands the neuroscience background and positioning of associative memory models. The discussion adds connections to transformer memory and factual-recall research, including Bietti et al. and Nichani et al., and situates single-layer ICL relative to linear-regression work by Zhang et al. and Lu et al.

P1.justification: Previously continuous sections are reorganized into named subsections separating setup, architecture, evaluation, interpretation, limitations, and conclusions. AMICL motivation and the discussion receive extensive explanatory expansion. The 8M model is renamed a toy language model, and the appendix structure is reorganized around new background and controls.

P2.justification: v2 adds training and benchmark plots, four control-experiment figures, and two hyperparameter tables. Figure 3's loss panel is revised, including its vertical scale. Original appendix Figures 4–6 and Tables 3–4 are retained as Figures 11–13 and Tables 5–6, alongside substantial figure-placement and layout changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical support beyond synthetic tasks and four simple IOI templates in 8M models. The 1B benchmarks, harder contextual retrieval task, and failed architectural controls provide stronger evidence about applicability and design limitations. Explicit discussion of task-specific gains improves calibration. Checkpoint-based significance testing, missing independent 1B training repetitions, and reporting inconsistencies limit confidence, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and explanation.
